column2: The White Hart
The White Bear
The White Tiger
The White Lion

For weeks now the charcoal burners, the woodcutters and the pedlars on the forest roads have told the same tale: a white hart walks the deep woods of my realm, tall as a warhorse, its antlers like a crown of bone. The peasants say it is an omen, that it cannot be wounded by common iron, and that whoever brings it down will never again miss a mark.

For weeks now the trappers and the herders have told the same tale: a white bear walks the frozen wilds of my realm, larger than any bear they have known, and it leaves no tracks in the snow. The old women say it is a beast from beyond the ice, and that whoever brings it down will carry its strength for the rest of their days.

For weeks now the villagers at the edge of the jungle have told the same tale: a white tiger hunts in the green dark of my realm, pale as moonlight and silent as death. They have stopped going out alone. The shamans say the beast is a spirit wearing flesh, and that whoever brings it down will take its cunning for their own.

For weeks now the herdsmen and the caravan guards have told the same tale: a white lion hunts the hills and the dry country of my realm, its mane bright as a cloud at noon. It has taken cattle and once a careless guard. The storytellers say that it is no mortal beast, and that whoever brings it down will be feared as it is feared.

The foresters bring word that the White Hart has been seen in the deep woods of my realm. Every child of the forest knows the tale: the White Hart is the Lord of the Wild's own beast, and where it walks the old god himself is watching. To hunt it is to be tested by the god. To kill it... the foresters do not say what happens to those who kill it. They only make the sign of the antlers and look away.

The trappers bring word that a white bear walks the snows of my realm, bigger than any bear of the oblast. The old women at the hearths already have a name for it: Ursun's child, sent by the Father of Bears to see whether the people of Kislev still remember him. To meet it is a great sign. To kill it would be a great sin, and a greater feat.

The shepherds of the high valleys bring word that a white lion walks the slopes above my lands. In Chrace a youth becomes a hunter in truth only when they have faced a great lion with nothing but an axe and their nerve, and the White Lions of the Phoenix King's guard still wear the pelts of the beasts they slew. Here is a test worthy of the oldest rite.
Send out the trackers. I want to know where it walks.
I have no time for peasants' tales.
Good news, my [Root.GetLordLady]! Woodsmen have seen the white hart in [hunting_beast_county.GetName], and its tracks are fresh. If we ride now we may yet find it.
Good news, my [Root.GetLordLady]! Trappers have seen the white bear in [hunting_beast_county.GetName], and it has killed a pack of wolves there. If we ride now we may yet find it.

Good news, my [Root.GetLordLady]! The white tiger has been seen in [hunting_beast_county.GetName]. It killed a water buffalo at the river and dragged it into the trees. If we go now we may yet find it.
Good news, my [Root.GetLordLady]! Herdsmen have seen the white lion in [hunting_beast_county.GetName], and it has taken two of their goats. If we ride now we may yet find it.
Ready the hounds and the spears!
Not now. There are more pressing matters.

In the chase I become separated from my companions and find myself alone in a clearing I do not know. Through the trees, something pale moves... a hart, as white as fresh snow, with a crown of antlers that catches the light. It looks straight at me. Then it turns and is gone, and though I spur after it I find not a single print in the moss.\n\nWhen I find my party again I say nothing. But I cannot stop thinking about it.

In the chase I become separated from my companions and find myself alone on a ridge of ice and stone. Below me something huge moves through the snow... a bear, white as the snow itself, bigger than any bear I have ever seen. It lifts its head and looks at me. Then it is gone into the blowing snow, and though I follow I find nothing.\n\nWhen I find my party again I say nothing. But I cannot stop thinking about it.

In the chase I become separated from my companions and find myself alone in the dripping green. The birds have gone silent. On a fallen trunk above me lies a tiger, pale as bone, its striped tail flicking. It watches me for a long moment, then flows away into the leaves without a sound.\n\nWhen I find my party again I say nothing. But I cannot stop thinking about it.

In the chase I become separated from my companions and find myself alone among rocks and dry grass. On a ledge above me stands a lion, white from mane to tail, gazing down as a king gazes at a beggar. Then it turns and is gone over the ridge, and though I climb after it I find nothing.\n\nWhen I find my party again I say nothing. But I cannot stop thinking about it.
The hounds are straining at their leashes, the spears are sharp and the trackers have their orders. Somewhere out there in the deep woods the white hart is waiting. It is time to ride.
The hounds are straining at their leashes, the spears are sharp and the trackers have their orders. Somewhere out there in the snows the white bear is waiting. It is time to ride.
The beaters are ready, the spears are sharp and the trackers have their orders. Somewhere out there in the green dark the white tiger is waiting. It is time to go.
The hounds are straining at their leashes, the spears are sharp and the trackers have their orders. Somewhere out there in the hills the white lion is waiting. It is time to ride.
A hunt for the ages!
This time it will not escape me!

After many days of tracking, the hounds drive the white hart into a hollow between two rocks with no way out. It turns to face me. Its flanks heave, its antlers are lowered, and its dark eyes hold mine with something that is almost understanding. It is the most beautiful thing I have ever seen.

After many days of tracking, the white bear is cornered at last against a frozen cliff. It rears up, twice the height of a man, and roars until the ice shakes. Then it drops to all fours and looks at me, and I could swear there is intelligence in that look.

After many days of tracking, the beaters drive the white tiger into a gully choked with vines. It crouches, snarling, and then goes still and looks at me with pale gold eyes. It knows, as I know, that it is at my mercy.
After many days of tracking, the white lion is trapped in a dry ravine with no way out. It turns, mane bristling, and roars a challenge. Then it falls silent and stares at me, proud even now.

After many days of tracking, the White Hart stands before me in a hollow with no way out. It does not flee. It lowers its antlers, and its dark eyes hold mine. The foresters with me have fallen to their knees. One of them is weeping. If this is the Lord of the Wild's own beast, then this moment is his test of me, and I alone must choose how to answer it.

After many days of tracking, Ursun's child is cornered against a frozen cliff. It rears up, roaring, and then drops to all fours and looks at me as an old bear looks at a cub. My huntsmen have lowered their spears and are muttering prayers to the Father of Bears. No one wants to strike the first blow. All eyes are on me.

After many days of tracking, the white lion is trapped in a dry ravine. It turns and roars, and my huntsmen fall back to leave the space between us clear, as the rite demands. Only my axe and my nerve now. This is how the hunters of Chrace have proved themselves since before Aenarion. Its pelt would make a cloak worthy of the Phoenix King's own guard.
Its head will adorn my hall!
I cannot slay such a noble beast. Let it go.
The beast does not run. It follows you home.

The trail leads me to the edge of a deep gorge. On the far side stands the white hart, staring back at me, close enough that I can see its breath steaming. There is no way across. As it turns and walks unhurriedly into the trees I know that I must go home empty-handed... this time.

The trail leads me to the edge of a deep crevasse in the ice. On the far side stands the white bear, staring back at me. There is no way across. As it turns and lumbers away into the snow I know that I must go home empty-handed... this time.

The trail leads me to the edge of a deep gorge with a river roaring far below. On the far side lies the white tiger, watching me and lazily licking a paw. There is no way across. As it rises and slips away into the leaves I know that I must go home empty-handed... this time.

The trail leads me to the edge of a deep gorge. On the far side stands the white lion, staring back at me. There is no way across. As it turns and pads away over the ridge I know that I must go home empty-handed... this time.
Now I know my purpose in life!
I will catch it some day.

Scouring the wilds for my prey, I come across a lone hunter, weathered and scarred, with a bow over his shoulder and a necklace of claws round his neck. As we talk it becomes clear that he has been tracking the very same beast for years. He has had no more luck than I, but he knows the land, and he offers to share what he has learned.
Come to my court. We will hunt it together.
I hunt alone.
A rival! He will not take my prize.
The rival hunter is never seen again.

I spend weeks in the wilderness searching for any sign of the beast, without the slightest success. I find plenty of biting flies, snakes, cold rain and saddle sores, however, and I am beginning to hate every tree in the realm.
This is pointless...

I spend weeks in the wilderness without finding any sign of the beast. And yet I find I do not mind. Sleeping under the stars, riding all day, eating what we catch... I feel leaner and stronger than I have in years.
This is the life!
I spend weeks in the wilderness searching for the beast and come home empty-handed. Nobody at court says a word about it, which is somehow worse.
It was my own failure.
My huntsmen are useless!

Fruitlessly searching the wilds, I come upon a crooked cottage half-buried in the undergrowth, with bundles of herbs and small bones hanging from the eaves. An old crone opens the door before I can knock. She looks me up and down, cackles, and says she has just the potion for a hunter like me: one draught and no prey will ever escape me again. For a price, of course.
Sell it to me!
No. We are going home.
Seize the witch! She will answer to the Order.

I drink the potion down in one draught. A warmth spreads from my belly to my fingertips, and the crone whispers: "See? I knew it. You will be a great hunter. Now go!"\n\nI ride home certain that next time the beast will not escape me.

I drink the potion down in one draught. Soon the cottage begins to spin, and then everything goes dark. When I wake I have a splitting headache and no wish to go on with the hunt. The crone is gone, and my guards swear they never saw her leave.
I do not feel well...
This feels good...
I have returned to court. The white beast has eluded me once more, but it is out there somewhere, and I will find it.
I will not give up.

Fruitlessly searching the wilds, I come upon a small cottage in a clearing. A beautiful young woman opens the door, looks at me for a long moment, and smiles. "It gets very lonely out here," she says. "Will you stay the night?"

Fruitlessly searching the wilds, I come upon a small cottage in a clearing. A handsome young man opens the door, looks at me for a long moment, and smiles. "It gets very lonely out here," he says. "Will you stay the night?"
How could I refuse?
I really should not.
It is a trap! Kill them!
You kill the treacherous stranger!\n

I wake the next morning with a warm body beside me. It was a long and very pleasant night, but the world outside is waiting. My companion runs a hand along my arm and asks me, softly, to stay just a little longer...
This was lovely, but I have to go.
Come back to court with me!

The wild knows what I am. Wherever my hunt rides, the birds fall silent and the deer scatter a mile ahead of us. The horses sweat and roll their eyes, the hounds whine and will not take the scent, and the white beast is long gone. But smoke rises from a charcoal burner's hut in the clearing below, and the old hunger stirs.

The beasts of the land fled from the chariots of the priest-kings in the age of glory, and they flee from them still. My skeletal huntsmen march without rest and without sound, but no living thing will wait to be found by the dead. For days the white beast has kept a valley ahead of us, never tiring, never turning.

The white beast does not flee from me as it would from a mortal hunter. It simply ceases to be where I am. The trees bend away from my path, the streams run backwards, and the beaters I took from the villages have begun to weep and pray to gods who will not help them. Still I can taste the beast's fear on the wind.
Send the dead to drive it. They do not tire, and they do not stop.
Hunt it through the Warp, where it cannot hide.
Let the beast run. There is warmer prey in the clearing.
Raise the bones of the beasts of old, and hunt as the kings of Nehekhara hunted.
Let the beast run. The villagers will make better sport.
The beast can wait. It will be here when I return.
My [GetFromRelation], [From.GetTitledFirstName], has sent me a gift: a puppy, all paws and ears, of the finest hunting stock. The kennel master says it will grow into a magnificent hound.

My [GetFromRelation], [From.GetTitledFirstName], has sent me a gift: a wolf cub, snatched from the pens of the wolf riders. It has already bitten the grot who carried it. It will grow up into a fine big beast.
What a gift!
Send it back.
Have someone quietly get rid of it...
The new pup has no name yet, my [Root.GetLordLady]. What will you call it?
Faithful.
Hunter.
Tricky.
Karanak, for the Hound of the Blood God.
Karanak
[Root.GetDogName] is growing fast and is no puppy any more. He runs fast, has a keen nose, and the kennel masters praise his good temper.
[Root.GetDogName] is growing fast and is no puppy any more. He runs fast and has a keen nose. He bites hard too, as several of the kennel boys can testify.
Good dog!
Hmm...
[Root.GetDogName] is always at my side, and always glad to see me. Whatever else happens at court, there is one creature here who asks nothing of me.
If only people were as loyal.
Everyone at court loves [Root.GetDogName]. The huntsmen praise him over their ale, and the children of the court spend whole afternoons chasing him round the yard.
And he loves them all.
[Root.GetDogName] needs proper training if he is to be any use on the hunt. Perhaps I should see to it myself?
Yes, I will train him myself.
No, the kennel masters are paid for that.
For months I have spent every spare hour out of doors training [Root.GetDogName]. The daily exercise and the fresh air have done wonders for my health and my temper.
[Root.GetDogName], fetch!
[Root.GetDogName] broke loose and ran wild through the hall. He chased the servants screaming from the kitchens, and then he found the lapdog of one of my courtiers and tore it to pieces.
Unfortunate.
At court today [Root.GetDogName] suddenly flew into a rage, tore free of his handler and leapt at one of my courtiers!
Heel! HEEL!
Kill! Kill!

[Root.GetDogName] has taken his last breath. He came to me as a clumsy puppy and served me faithfully all his life, at the hunt and at my feet by the fire. Now it is time to lay my old friend to rest.
I will bury him quietly under the old oak.
He deserves a proper funeral.
A pyramid for [Root.GetDogName]!
Embalm him and raise a pyramid. He will guard my tomb for eternity.
Poor Karanak!
Antlers of the White Hart
The great antlers of a white hart of legend, mounted above the high seat. Pale as bone and branched like a crown, they draw every guest's eye.
Pelt of the White Beast
The pale pelt of a beast out of legend, worn as a cloak. Peasants touch its hem for luck when their lord rides by.

The horns sound in the courtyard, the hounds bay in their leashes and the whole court rides out behind me into the deep forests. For two months we will hunt stag and boar under the old trees, sleep in pavilions and feast on what we kill, and pray that nothing older than the boar is hunting us.

The horns sound across the snow, the hounds strain at their leashes and the whole court rides out behind me into the frozen pine forests. For two months we will hunt elk and bear and wolf, sleep in fur tents and feast on what we kill.

The horns sound at dawn, the hawks shift on their perches and the whole court rides out behind me towards the oases and the dry hills. For two months we will hunt gazelle and lion, sleep in silk tents and feast on what we kill.
To the hunt!
In a clearing at dawn stands a stag such as the huntsmen speak of in their cups: twenty points on its antlers, as tall at the shoulder as my horse. It lifts its head and looks straight at me.
A noble beast. I will remember it.
It is looking at me... Back away slowly.
Lower the bows. Let it live.
After it! That head will hang in my hall.

An arrow hummed past my ear this morning and buried itself in a tree. The huntsmen swore it was a stray. Now every rustle in the bracken sounds like a bowstring, and every face in the hunting party looks like a murderer's.
I will not hide from my own court. Ride on.
I will keep them all where I can see them.
Your bow is ready if anyone moves.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] is dead, an arrow through [From.GetHerHis] throat in the deep woods. A tragic accident of the hunt, everyone agrees. The huntsmen are searching the bracken for the careless archer, and will not find [Root.GetHerHim].
Such a tragedy.

The arrow that struck me was no stray. Someone in my hunting party wants me dead, and missed. I bound the wound myself and rode back at the head of the hunt as if nothing had happened, and I watched their faces as I did.
Next time they had better not miss.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] has been watching me all day. In the deep woods, with no one near, [From.GetSheHe] turned in [From.GetHerHis] saddle, drew and loosed before I could reach my own bow.
No!

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has been watching me strangely all day. In the deep woods I reached for my quiver, and [From.GetSheHe] turned in [From.GetHerHis] saddle and loosed an arrow straight at me. I never did anything to [From.GetHerHim].
Why?
The hounds have run a great hart to a standstill against a cliff. It is old and grey about the muzzle, the king of these woods for years. The huntsmen look to me for the killing shot.
It has earned its freedom. Call off the hounds.
Give the shot to my finest huntsman.
I will take it myself.
A great boar has burst out of the thicket, tusks like daggers and eyes red with fury. It tore open two hounds before anyone could blink, and now it has turned to face the hunt.
Let the huntsmen deal with it.
Give me the boar spear!
A bear has risen up on its hind legs in front of my horse, twice the height of a man. The horse screams and dances, the hounds have scattered, and for one long moment it is just me and the beast.
Hold still and let it pass.
Spear!
Run!
The kennel master has brought out a new pack, lean and scarred, bred from the war hounds of the frontier. He says they will take down anything that runs. He also says he cannot always call them back.
I will run with them myself.
Let them loose!
Take them back to the kennels.
The hounds may run where they should not.
The new hounds broke away from the hunt and ran down a peasant gathering wood at the forest edge. There was not much left of him when the huntsmen caught up. His family is waiting at the castle gate.
Pay the family for their loss.
He should not have been in my woods.
My horse went lame in a rabbit hole, miles from camp. The rest of the hunt has ridden on.
I will lead it home on foot.
Fetch a servant to carry me back!
After a long day of chasing nothing, the hounds flushed a hare and I brought it down with a lucky arrow. Not much of a trophy, but the cooks are pleased.
Better than nothing!
Three days in the saddle and I have not killed so much as a rabbit. My arrows fly wide, my spear finds only mud, and I can hear the huntsmen sniggering behind me.
Laugh with them. I am no hunter.
The huntsmen scared off the game!
The beaters have driven a great beast into a gully, and the huntsmen are setting the nets and spears to take it safely. I have killed a hundred beasts. I do not need nets.
Stand aside. This one is mine.
...On second thought, set the nets.
I brought down the quarry today, a clean shot through the heart, with [Root.Liege.GetTitledFirstName] still a field behind. The whole hunt saw it.
I lay it at my [Root.Liege.GetLordLady]'s feet.
The finest shot of the season, and it was mine!
[From.GetTitledFirstName] killed my quarry before I could, and then made a great show of laying it at my feet. The whole court is smirking.
Throw [From.GetHerHim] in the dungeon for poaching!
A good shot is a good shot.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] killed my quarry before I could and has been boasting about it ever since, at every fire and over every cup.
Let [From.GetHerHim] have [From.GetHerHis] moment.

[hunt_park_vassal.GetTitledFirstName] has ridden with the hunt every day and admired my deer park at length. Now [hunt_park_vassal.GetSheHe] asks for a herd of my deer to stock [hunt_park_vassal.GetHerHis] own woods. My steward says the treasury could bear it.
My deer stay in my park.
Send [hunt_park_vassal.GetHerHim] a herd.
It is not worth the trouble of rounding them up.
A rider caught up with the hunt this morning: we are at war. The hounds were called in, the pavilions struck and the court rode home in silence.
Back to the castle.
The last horn has sounded and the hunt rides home, laden with antlers, pelts and stories that will grow taller every winter.
A fine hunt.
Tusks of a Great Boar
The yellowed tusks of a great boar taken at a grand hunt, mounted on an oak plaque. The scar on the hunter's leg is a matching souvenir.
Bearskin Cloak
The skin of a great bear killed with a spear at a grand hunt, its head worn as a hood. Children run from it.
You have decided to organize a tiger hunt. You will invite your vassals to enjoy this occasion with you.

Dear vassal,

I am organizing a great tiger hunt for all my vassals, and hereby invite you to attend.

[From.GetFullName]

My liege,

Unfortunately, I have pressing business that forces me to decline your invitation to the tiger hunt.

[From.GetFullName]

You have arrived at the hunting camp. Retainers are available to see to your every need, and soldiers will be useful both for guarding the camp and for flushing out any tigers. This should be a fine day!

The hunters and their respective entourages have gathered at the hunting camp. Retainers are available to see to your every need, and soldiers will be useful both for guarding the camp and for flushing out any tigers. This should be a fine day!

The social life at the camp is an important part of the tiger hunt. Late at night, after many cups of wine and Arabyan date spirit, you sit and talk into the small hours. You are having a good time, and it seems you have made a new friend.

The social life at the camp is an important part of the tiger hunt. Late at night, after many cups of wine and Arabyan date spirit, you sit and talk into the small hours. But misunderstandings occur so easily among the inebriated...

Evening pastimes during the tiger hunt include playing at cards. A group has gathered to play and you join them. Of course, the game is only interesting if you play for gold and silver - but how much will you bet?
The card game didn't go very well, and you lost a significant amount of money.
You had mixed fortunes at the card game, and in the end your wins and losses balanced out.
You had an excellent run at the card game, and won a significant amount of money.

The hunting party pushes through the steaming jungle and the thorn scrub. You are hoping luck will find you a tiger to kill. Suddenly, there is a movement in the underbrush... and a large tiger springs out, roaring fiercely! It attacks the hunting party, but soldiers immediately move to attack it and they manage to kill it with their spears.

The hunting party pushes through the steaming jungle and the thorn scrub. You are hoping luck will find you a tiger to kill. Suddenly, there is a movement in the underbrush... and a large tiger springs out, roaring fiercely! It attacks the hunting party, striking at one of the servants, ripping him to shreds before disappearing again into the jungle.

The hunting party pushes through the steaming jungle and the thorn scrub. You are hoping luck will find you a tiger to kill. Suddenly, there is a movement in the underbrush... and a large tiger springs out, roaring fiercely! It attacks the hunting party, striking at one of the hunters, ripping and tearing flesh before disappearing again into the jungle.
Several forward scouts come running back to the main hunting party. In excited whispers, they inform you that a large tiger has been spotted ahead.

Stepping forward, you watch the tiger closely, weighing your spear in your hand and waiting for the right moment to strike. The tiger prowls towards you, slowly. Then suddenly, it leaps towards you! You sidestep and stab with your spear, sinking it deeply into its flank.

Stepping forward, you watch the tiger closely, weighing your spear in your hand and waiting for the right moment to strike. The tiger prowls towards you, slowly. Then suddenly, the huge beast stops, looking nervous. It turns and runs into the dense vegetation before you can throw your spear.

Stepping forward, you watch the tiger closely, weighing your spear in your hand and waiting for the right moment to strike. Then suddenly, the tiger leaps towards you! Surprised, you stumble backwards as it starts to tear at you with claws and teeth. Your soldiers run in, stabbing at the beast, and it decides to retreat, disappearing into the dense vegetation.

The hunting party edges forward, encircling the area and closing on the tiger. The beast discovers the trap too late and tries to run, but the hunters close in from all sides, stabbing with their spears. The tiger roars wildly as its life's blood spills over the ground.

The hunting party edges forward, encircling the area and closing on the tiger. The beast, however, smells the trap and turns and flees into the dense vegetation. Several soldiers run after it but return shortly after to report that the animal is gone.
A most successful hunt! A slain tiger means luck for the realm and everyone heads for home with new optimism.
A failed hunt! No tigers were slain, and this is an ill omen for the realm. You vow to return and have better luck next time.
Send riders with the invitations.
A tiger hunt! Of course I will go.
'Pressing business', eh?
I can't wait!
I can't wait!
Good times!
I hate you!
Play with high stakes.
I knew I shouldn't have played!
Oh well.
I'm good at this!
Phew, that was close!
No!
Hand me my spear, and stand back. I will kill it myself.
I killed the tiger!
I failed to kill the tiger!
I have been grievously wounded!
We killed the tiger!
No luck today, it seems.
Rejoice!
Unfortunate.
I have no time for sport.
Play with low stakes.
Bring the soldiers forward, let's corner it and kill it.
Pelt of the Great Cat
The striped hide of a tiger speared at a great hunt in the south, its head still snarling over the wearer's shoulder. Courtiers give it a wide berth.
The invitations are sent.
A reply is sent to [From.GetFullName].
